cls: Vesicular monoamine transporter 2 (VMAT2) inhibitor - monoamine depleting agent
quick: Start 12.5 mg/day; titrate weekly to control chorea (usual 12.5-50 mg/day)
May be taken with or without food
Limited data; use only if clearly needed
Not studied in renal impairment; use caution
summary: Tetrabenazine is a reversible VMAT2 inhibitor that depletes presynaptic monoamines (especially dopamine) and is used to treat chorea associated with Huntington disease. It carries an important risk of depression and suicidality, can prolong the QT interval, and is metabolized to active forms by CYP2D6, requiring lower maximum doses in poor metabolizers and with strong CYP2D6 inhibitors. It is contraindicated in hepatic impairment and in actively suicidal or untreated depressed patients.
indications: Treatment of chorea associated with Huntington disease

dosage.n: Increase to 12.5 mg twice daily after one week
Titrate slowly to tolerability; doses >37.5 mg/day given in 3 divided doses

dosage.d: Up to 100 mg/day total (max single dose 37.5 mg)

dosage.c: Chorea - poor CYP2D6 metabolizers or with strong CYP2D6 inhibitor
dosage.d: Max 50 mg/day total (max single dose 25 mg)
dosage.n: Reduced maximum due to elevated active metabolite levels

admin: Titrate slowly to identify the dose that reduces chorea and is well tolerated
Divide doses three times daily when total exceeds 37.5 mg/day
If treatment is interrupted for more than 5 days, re-titrate from the starting dose
moa: Tetrabenazine reversibly inhibits vesicular monoamine transporter type 2 (VMAT2), reducing uptake of monoamines (dopamine, serotonin, norepinephrine, histamine) into synaptic vesicles and depleting their presynaptic stores. The resulting reduction in central dopaminergic transmission decreases the excessive involuntary movements (chorea) of Huntington disease.

absolute: Active suicidal ideation or untreated/inadequately treated depression
Concomitant use with monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) or within 14 days of stopping an MAOI
Concomitant use with reserpine (allow 20 days washout)
relative: History of depression or suicide attempt
Congenital long QT syndrome or arrhythmias

preg: There are limited human data. Tetrabenazine should be used during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus; animal data are limited.
lact: It is not known whether tetrabenazine is excreted in human milk. Because of the potential for serious adverse reactions in the nursing infant, breastfeeding is not recommended during therapy.
renal: Tetrabenazine has not been evaluated in patients with renal impairment; use with caution.
hepatic: Contraindicated in patients with hepatic impairment, in whom drug exposure is substantially increased.

major: MAO inhibitors (contraindicated - risk of hypertensive crisis/serotonin effects)
Strong CYP2D6 inhibitors e.g. paroxetine, fluoxetine, quinidine (raise active metabolites - limit dose to 50 mg/day)
QT-prolonging drugs (additive QT prolongation - arrhythmia risk)
moderate: Dopamine antagonists / antipsychotics (additive risk of parkinsonism, NMS, akathisia)
interactions.alcohol: Avoid - additive CNS depression and sedation

serious: Tardive dyskinesia (less common than with antipsychotics)
emergency: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (hyperthermia, rigidity, autonomic instability)
Serious cardiac arrhythmia from QT prolongation

monitoring: Depression and suicidal ideation/behavior at each visit
ECG for QT interval, especially with dose increases or QT-prolonging co-meds
Signs of parkinsonism, akathisia, dysphagia, and NMS
counsel: Watch for and immediately report worsening mood, depression, or thoughts of self-harm
Do not stop abruptly without medical advice; if doses are missed for more than 5 days the drug must be re-started at a low dose
Avoid alcohol and other sedating substances
Report fainting, palpitations, fever with muscle stiffness, or difficulty swallowing
Drowsiness may impair driving and operating machinery
pk: Reduction in chorea develops over the titration period (days to weeks)
Active metabolites (alpha- and beta-dihydrotetrabenazine) peak ~1-1.5 hours after dosing
Active dihydrotetrabenazine metabolites ~4-8 hours (parent drug very short)
Short - typically dosed two to three times daily
Store at controlled room temperature 20-25 C
pearls: Extensively converted by CYP2D6 to active dihydrotetrabenazine metabolites; poor metabolizers and strong CYP2D6 inhibitors require a 50 mg/day cap
Carries a notable risk of depression and suicidality - screen mood before and during therapy
Can prolong the QT interval - avoid stacking with other QT-prolonging drugs
Contraindicated with MAOIs and reserpine and in hepatic impairment
Deutetrabenazine and valbenazine are newer VMAT2 inhibitors with longer half-lives
missed: Take a missed dose as soon as remembered unless it is near the next scheduled dose, in which case skip it. If therapy has been interrupted for more than 5 days, do not resume the previous dose - the drug must be re-titrated from the starting dose under medical supervision.
overdose: Reported overdose effects include acute dystonia, oculogyric crisis, nausea, vomiting, sweating, sedation, hypotension, confusion, diarrhea, hallucinations, tremor, and rubor. Treatment is supportive; monitor cardiac rhythm (QT) and vital signs and treat symptomatically.
